title: Diabetic Foot: Risk Stratification and Ulcer Referral

teaching.scope: Adults with diabetes in primary care and hospital: foot risk stratification and review intervals, referral to foot protection or multidisciplinary foot care, ulcer, infection and Charcot assessment, and antibiotic choice for infection. Checked against NICE NG19 recommendations 1.1.3, 1.3.3–1.3.13, 1.4.1–1.4.2, 1.5.1–1.5.5, 1.6.1–1.6.12 and 1.7.1–1.7.8 with Tables 1–2, and the Saudi Diabetes Clinical Practice Guidelines diabetic foot section (printed pp. 81–82).
pitfalls: Assuming a hot swollen foot with intact skin is infection or gout and missing Charcot.
Normal X-ray, inflammatory markers or probe-to-bone excluding osteomyelitis.
Using total contact casting on an ischaemic or infected ulcer.
keyPoints: Active problem: referral within 1 working day; limb- or life-threatening: immediately to acute services.
Review every 3–6 months moderate, 1–2 months high.
Do not use the Wagner score; use SINBAD or University of Texas.
Samples before antibiotics; review IV at 48 hours.

references.title: NICE NG19: Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management
Saudi Diabetes Clinical Practice Guidelines (Saudi National Diabetes Center / Saudi Health Council)

learningObjectives: Stratify diabetic foot risk and set the correct review interval and referral timing.
Recognise a limb-threatening or active foot problem and choose antibiotics by infection severity.

redFlags: Ulceration with fever or sepsis, ulceration with limb ischaemia, suspected deep soft tissue or bone infection, or gangrene: refer immediately to acute services and tell the multidisciplinary foot care service (NG19 1.4.1).
Any other active diabetic foot problem: refer within 1 working day to the multidisciplinary foot care or foot protection service for triage within 1 further working day (NG19 1.4.2).
Suspected acute Charcot arthropathy (red, warm, swollen foot, especially with intact skin): refer within 1 working day and keep non-weight-bearing (NG19 1.7.2–1.7.3).
Severe infection with systemic signs (temperature above 38 °C or below 36 °C, raised heart rate or respiratory rate): intravenous antibiotics and urgent assessment (NG19 terms used, Table 2).
symptoms: Numbness, burning or pain in the feet (SDCPG p. 81).
A hot, swollen foot with change in colour, with or without pain (NG19 1.3.6, 1.7.2).
Fever, rigors or spreading redness around a wound (NG19 1.4.1).
precipitants: Previous ulceration or amputation, renal replacement therapy, neuropathy with peripheral arterial disease, or neuropathy or arterial disease with callus or deformity (high risk, NG19 1.3.6).
Smoking, retinopathy and renal disease (SDCPG p. 81).
physicalSigns: Neuropathy on 10 g monofilament sensation testing (NG19 1.3.4; SDCPG p. 82).
Pedal pulses and limb ischaemia; ankle-brachial index if pulses are reduced (NG19 1.3.4–1.3.5; SDCPG p. 82).
Ulcer, callus, deformity, gangrene, Charcot changes and signs of infection (NG19 1.3.4).
Infection defined by at least 2 of local swelling or induration, erythema, tenderness or pain, warmth or purulent discharge (NG19 terms used).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Hot, red, swollen foot with intact skin and neuropathy; confirm with weight-bearing X-ray and MRI if X-ray normal (NG19 1.7.2, 1.7.4).
Local infection, deep or chronic wound; may be present with normal inflammatory markers, X-ray or probe-to-bone test; MRI if X-ray not confirmatory (NG19 1.6.3–1.6.5).
Ulceration or gangrene with limb ischaemia needs immediate acute services (NG19 1.4.1).

differentials.condition: Gout, trauma, fracture, thrombosis or venous stasis
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Other causes of an inflamed foot are excluded before calling mild infection (NG19 terms used).

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with diabetes in primary care and hospital: foot risk stratification and review intervals, referral to foot protection or multidisciplinary foot care, ulcer, infection and Charcot assessment, and antibiotic choice for infection. Checked against NICE NG19 recommendations 1.1.3, 1.3.3–1.3.13, 1.4.1–1.4.2, 1.5.1–1.5.5, 1.6.1–1.6.12 and 1.7.1–1.7.8 with Tables 1–2, and the Saudi Diabetes Clinical Practice Guidelines diabetic foot section (printed pp. 81–82).
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 14 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: The SDCPG gives annual foot examination and referral for claudication or reduced pulses but no risk categories or review intervals; the categories and intervals here are NICE NG19.
NG19 is a UK guideline; the foot protection service and multidisciplinary foot care service need local equivalents in Saudi hospitals.
Antibiotic doses are the NICE NG19 table doses; the product labels were not opened, so label contraindications are not verified, and Pseudomonas and MRSA regimens are not reproduced.
Saudi antimicrobial resistance patterns were not assessed; follow the local antibiogram.
SFDA registration and hospital formulary availability were not independently verified.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Neuropathy, ischaemia, deformity, callus, prior ulcer or amputation place the person in moderate, high or active categories (NG19 1.3.4, 1.3.6).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Remove shoes, socks and dressings and examine both feet; SDCPG advises at least annual foot examination and more often in high risk (NG19 1.3.3–1.3.4; SDCPG p. 81).

ruleIn.normalValue: No bone destruction, fracture or Charcot change
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Adult with suspected infection, osteomyelitis or acute Charcot arthropathy
ruleIn.expectedFinding: X-ray shows the extent of the problem; MRI if osteomyelitis or Charcot is suspected but the X-ray is normal (NG19 1.6.2, 1.6.5, 1.7.4).

ruleIn.testName: Foot-skin temperature difference with serial weight-bearing X-ray
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Skin temperature at the same site on both feet; X-ray of the foot and ankle, MRI if the X-ray is normal
ruleIn.normalValue: Difference between the two feet of less than 2 °C, with no further change on X-ray
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Red, warm, swollen foot with intact skin, especially with neuropathy or renal failure; a sustained temperature difference of 2 °C or more means the Charcot process is still active
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Suspected Charcot: refer to the multidisciplinary foot care service within 1 working day and offer non-weight-bearing treatment. Treatment is likely to be complete when the difference stays under 2 °C and X-rays show no further progression.

medicationPlan.note: Antibiotic doses and course lengths are NICE NG19 Table 1 (mild) and Table 2 (moderate or severe) for adults 18 and over; seek specialist advice for under 18 (NG19 1.6.9). Doses must be adjusted for renal or hepatic impairment, pregnancy and breastfeeding per the BNF. Pseudomonas and MRSA cover are given in the guideline and are not reproduced here. SFDA registration was not verified. Check hospital formulary and local antibiogram.

pathophysiology.summary: Peripheral neuropathy removes protective sensation, peripheral arterial disease reduces perfusion, and deformity concentrates pressure; together they cause ulceration, infection and amputation (SDCPG p. 81; NG19 terms used). Risk is graded low, moderate, high or active by the combination of neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease, deformity, callus, prior ulcer or amputation and renal replacement therapy (NG19 1.3.6). Foot ulcers heal only when offloading, infection, ischaemia and wound care are all addressed by an interprofessional team (SDCPG p. 81; NG19 1.5.4). Charcot arthropathy follows foot or ankle fracture in neuropathy and presents as a hot, red, swollen foot with intact skin; early non-weight-bearing offloading limits deformity (NG19 1.7.1–1.7.3).

clinicalManagement.title: Triage for emergencies
actions: Immediate referral to acute services for ulcer with fever or sepsis, ulcer with ischaemia, suspected deep or bone infection, or gangrene (NG19 1.4.1).
Hospital inpatient with a foot problem: refer to the multidisciplinary foot care service within 24 hours of the first foot examination (NG19 1.1.3).

clinicalManagement.title: Examine and stratify risk
actions: Examine both feet with shoes and socks off; use a 10 g monofilament, check pulses, deformity, callus and signs of ulcer or infection (NG19 1.3.4; SDCPG p. 82).
Classify as low, moderate, high or active (NG19 1.3.6).
Reassess on any foot problem and on every hospital admission (NG19 1.3.3).
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At diagnosis and at least annually

clinicalManagement.title: Manage by category
actions: Low risk: annual review and foot-care education (NG19 1.3.7).
Moderate or high risk: refer to the foot protection service, seen within 6–8 weeks (moderate) or 2–4 weeks (high) (NG19 1.3.8–1.3.9).
Active problem not needing acute services: refer within 1 working day for triage within 1 further working day (NG19 1.4.2).
Review interval: 3–6 months moderate; 1–2 months high; 1–2 weeks if high with immediate concern (NG19 1.3.11).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat the ulcer
actions: Offer offloading, infection control, ischaemia control, debridement and dressings (NG19 1.5.4).
Offer non-removable casting for plantar neuropathic, non-ischaemic, uninfected forefoot and midfoot ulcers; use another offloading device until casting is available (NG19 1.5.5).

Do not use electrical stimulation, platelet-rich plasma gel, growth factors or hyperbaric oxygen outside a trial (NG19 1.5.12; SDCPG p. 82 agrees there is not sufficient evidence for routine growth factors).

clinicalManagement.title: Infection
actions: Take a sample from the base of the debrided wound, or a deep swab, then start antibiotics as soon as possible (NG19 1.6.1, 1.6.6).
Choose by severity, microbiology, previous antibiotics and preference; oral first line if possible; review IV at 48 hours (NG19 1.6.7, 1.6.10–1.6.11).
Think about osteomyelitis; X-ray, then MRI if not confirmed (NG19 1.6.2–1.6.5).
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as infection is suspected

clinicalManagement.title: Acute Charcot arthropathy
actions: Suspect with redness, warmth, swelling or deformity, especially with intact skin and neuropathy (NG19 1.7.2).
Refer within 1 working day and offer non-weight-bearing treatment until definitive treatment starts (NG19 1.7.3).
Weight-bearing X-ray, MRI if normal; non-removable offloading device; no bisphosphonates outside a trial; monitor skin temperature difference and serial X-rays (NG19 1.7.4–1.7.7).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: No risk factors except callus alone (NG19 1.3.6)
Deformity, or neuropathy, or peripheral arterial disease (NG19 1.3.6)
Previous ulcer or amputation; renal replacement therapy; neuropathy plus peripheral arterial disease; or neuropathy or peripheral arterial disease with callus and/or deformity (NG19 1.3.6)
Ulceration, infection, chronic limb-threatening ischaemia, gangrene, or suspected acute Charcot arthropathy or an unexplained hot, swollen foot (NG19 1.3.6)
Low: annually; moderate: every 3–6 months; high: every 1–2 months, or every 1–2 weeks if immediate concern (NG19 1.3.11)
Within 2–4 weeks if high risk; within 6–8 weeks if moderate risk (NG19 1.3.9)
Mild: erythema 0.5 to under 2 cm, skin and subcutaneous only; moderate: erythema over 2 cm or deeper structures; severe: systemic inflammatory response signs (NG19 terms used)

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Reassess at the interval set by risk category and review the treatment plan frequency by healing and deterioration (NG19 1.3.11, 1.5.13); high-risk feet from previous Charcot remain with the foot protection service (NG19 1.7.8).
mdtReferrals: Foot protection service led by a podiatrist for moderate and high risk (NG19 1.2.2, 1.3.8).
Multidisciplinary foot care service including diabetology, vascular surgery, microbiology, orthopaedics and wound care for active problems (NG19 1.2.3).
Vascular assessment and ABI for reduced pulses or claudication (NG19 1.3.5; SDCPG p. 82).
Biomechanics and orthotics for footwear and offloading (NG19 1.3.10).
lifestyleAndDiet: Wear properly tailored footwear if high risk (SDCPG p. 82).
Stop smoking and keep glucose and blood pressure in the agreed range (SDCPG p. 81).
Inspect both feet daily and keep skin and nails clean and cared for (NG19 1.3.10, 1.3.13).
patientEducation: Give oral and written information on basic foot care, footwear, foot emergencies and whom to contact, and the person's current risk level (NG19 1.3.13; SDCPG p. 82).
Explain the foot problem, care of the other foot and leg, wound care and why glucose control matters when a problem arises (NG19 1.4.3).
dischargeCriteria: Risk category and review interval documented and the referral date confirmed.
Offloading, wound care and antibiotic plan agreed with the person, with a review within 48 hours if IV antibiotics were given (NG19 1.6.11).
Foot emergency instructions and contact details given orally and in writing (NG19 1.3.13, 1.4.3).
